claims.text: A single or falling CRP result cannot alone exclude early-onset sepsis or determine whether to stop antibiotics. NICE NG195 requires that decisions to stop antibiotics take account of the level of initial clinical suspicion, the baby's clinical progress and current condition, and the levels and trends of C-reactive protein, not CRP in isolation.

For this 32-week infant at 24 hours of age, the CRP trend from 20 to 11 to 5 mg/L is a falling pattern. While the guideline notes that 'levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration' are a factor in antibiotic review, this trend must be interpreted alongside clinical indicators and initial suspicion, as CRP trends alone are insufficient to rule out infection.

If antibiotics are continued for more than 36 hours due to strong initial clinical suspicion, the baby should be reviewed at least once every 24 hours. At each review, the decision to stop antibiotics must consider the initial clinical suspicion, the baby's clinical progress and current condition, and the levels and trends of C-reactive protein.

The blood culture status is currently unknown. NICE NG195 specifies that stopping antibiotics at 36 hours requires a negative blood culture, in addition to reassuring clinical condition and CRP trends. The absence of a confirmed negative culture result means the criteria for early antibiotic cessation are not yet fully met.

For babies being treated with intravenous antibiotics due to risk factors or clinical indicators, C-reactive protein concentration should be measured 18 to 24 hours after starting antibiotics to establish a trend. This supports the guideline requirement to assess 'levels and trends of C-reactive protein' when reviewing antibiotic therapy.

The patient's red flags are noted as 'not fully documented.' Since the decision to stop antibiotics depends on the baby's clinical condition being reassuring with no clinical indicators of possible infection, incomplete documentation of red flags limits the ability to confirm that clinical criteria for antibiotic cessation are met.

evidence.text: If continuing antibiotics for longer than 48 hours for suspected late‑onset neonatal infection despite negative blood culture, review the baby at least once every 24 hours. At each review, decide whether to stop antibiotics, taking account of: • the level of initial clinical suspicion of infection and • the baby's clinical progress and current condition and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein. [2021]

For babies born from 35+0 weeks' gestation with negative blood culture who need antibiotics for more than 36 hours because the initial clinical suspicion of infection was strong, consider switching treatment from intravenous to oral antibiotics at 36 hours or thereafter to complete the course (up to 7 days of antibiotics in total) if: • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no current clinical indicators of ongoing infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection) and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring and • the baby is tolerating oral feeds. [2026]

For babies who are being treated with intravenous antibiotics because of risk factors for early-onset infection or clinical indicators of possible infection, stop antibiotics at 36 hours if: • the blood culture is negative and • the initial clinical suspicion of infection was not strong and • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no clinical indicators of possible infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset infection) and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring. [2012, amended 2026]

In babies given antibiotics because of risk factors for infection or clinical indicators of possible late-onset neonatal infection, measure the C reactive protein concentration 18 to 24 hours after starting antibiotics. [2021]
